title: When the owner pronoun can be left out
summary: First- and second-person endings already identify the owner, so minun, sinun, meidän, and teidän can be omitted: minun palloni or palloni both mean “my ball”.
targetSkills: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference
objectives: Omit a first- or second-person owner pronoun while keeping its noun ending.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: First- and second-person endings already identify the owner, so minun, sinun, meidän, and teidän can be omitted: minun palloni or palloni both mean “my ball”.
In Tämä on hänen pallonsa and Tämä on heidän pallonsa, retain the owner pronoun to say whose ball it is. Pallonsa alone does not tell us whether the intended owner is he, she, or they.

Third-person pronouns can be omitted in other sentence patterns when the suffix refers to that sentence’s actor. This pack does not practise those reference rules. Do not treat the rule for this basic frame as a rule for every Finnish sentence.
keyPoints: When the owner pronoun can be left out
Practise one singular possessed thing with the supporting forms shown.

steps: Pallo (“ball”) + -ni = palloni. The ending -ni already identifies “my”.
Omit minun from Tämä on minun palloni; keep the noun ending and Tämä on (“This is”).
Kirja (“book”) + -si = kirjasi. The ending -si identifies one owner addressed as “you”.
Omit sinun from Tämä on sinun kirjasi; the complete meaning remains “This is your book”.
Auto (“car”) + -mme = automme. The ending -mme already expresses “our”.
Omit meidän from Tämä on meidän automme. Keep both m letters and the singular identity frame Tämä on.
Peli (“game”) + -nne = pelinne. The ending -nne identifies a group addressed as “you”.
Omit teidän from Tämä on teidän pelinne. Keep both n letters; this differs from singular -si.
Kynä (“pen”) + -nsä = kynänsä. This ending is shared by single and group third-person owners.
Retain hänen (“her” or “his”) in this identity frame to identify the single owner; the model meaning uses “her”.
Tyyny (“pillow”) + -nsä = tyynynsä, with the same third-person ending used for a single owner.
Retain heidän (“their”) in this identity frame to distinguish several owners. Other sentence patterns have reference rules outside this lesson.

commonMistakes: When leaving out minun, sinun, meidän, or teidän, keep the possessive noun ending: palloni still means “my ball”.
Retain hänen or heidän in the independent identity sentences practised here; the shared third-person suffix alone does not identify the owner.
Follow the requested shorter or explicit form. Other sentence patterns have third-person reference rules outside this lesson.

practiceExercises.explanation: The ending on kynäsi already identifies the owner, so both the pronoun-free and explicit-pronoun sentences are natural.

parts.formation: Tämä is the supplied basic singular word for “this”.
Olla uses on because the thing being identified is singular; the owner can still be plural.
kynä + -si = kynäsi. The ending marks the owner, not several things.

answerDiagnostics.category: Possessive pronoun omission and clear reference: predictable form error
answerDiagnostics.explanation: In standard written Finnish, omitting the pronoun is possible here; omitting the possessive noun ending is not.

practiceExercises.explanation: Remove only teidän; keep autonne. The -nne ending identifies the owner.
